name: Notes and task apps as a filing target (Apple Notes, Obsidian, Things, Bear, Notion, Trello)
description: Six bundled skills teach an agent to file things into a notes or task app the parents already open on their phones. On this stack only two are worth building, and only as host-side wrappers: appending to a shared Apple Note, and opening the household vault in Obsidian as a reader.
example: 'Add the plumber's quote to the House note' or 'put the packing list in Notes so I can tick it off at the store'.
how:
The bundled skills are instruction packs for command-line tools (memo, obsidian, things, grizzly, ntn, curl) and assume exec, which no Happy agent has; an eligible skill grants no tool. Follow the F030 pattern instead: a small in-house plugin on

-main that runs a fixed command host-side. Apple Notes: not through memo, whose add and edit are interactive; the wrapper would be a few lines of AppleScript with Automation permission for Notes granted in happy's session, exposing only append-to-named-note and read-named-note (unverified, see below). Obsidian: the bundled memory-wiki plugin is described as an Obsidian-friendly vault, so the F043 folder can be opened in Obsidian with no agent tool at all. Things and Bear only if a parent already lives in them. Notion and Trello are API-token cloud services and are skipped.
depends_on: A shared Apple Note or folder that happy's Apple Account is invited to
caveats: memo adds and edits notes through an interactive editor and its skill warns that prompts may need a terminal, so a non-interactive append may have to use AppleScript directly.
The skill says notes that contain images or attachments cannot be edited.
The official obsidian CLI needs Obsidian 1.12.7 or later running in happy's desktop session.
Things database reads need Full Disk Access, updates need a Things auth token, and its CLI cannot delete.
Bear needs the app installed and running.
Shared Reminders (F030) already gives both phones a tick-off list; Notes adds free-form pages only.
Notion and Trello would be two more stores of family details outside the house.

memo adds and edits notes through $EDITOR and documents no flag or stdin input for note content, so it cannot drive an unattended append; the wrapper would be hand-written AppleScript, which no opened source covers.
memo needs Python 3.13 or later and its own README lists the project as under development.
safety:
A notes target is a write path for private data, so it belongs only on

-main, with the note or folder name fixed in plugin code, no delete, and the F041 rule that tainted runs cannot write. A note shared through iCloud is visible only to invited family members. Notion and Trello would send household content to third-party clouds under a token the Gateway holds, so they stay out.
unverified: Whether memo can append to an existing note without an interactive editor
Whether Automation permission for Notes can be granted to the launchd-run node process the same way as for Reminders
Which sync method for an Obsidian vault the family would accept on their phones
Whether an AppleScript append to a shared iCloud note works unattended from the Gateway's launchd session and preserves checklists and formatting

name: Grocery list to an Instacart link, parent checks out
description: Commercial assistants hand the grocery list to a delivery service. Happy can turn the Saturday list or the week's meal plan into one Instacart shopping-list link; a parent opens it, picks the store and pays. Happy never touches a cart.
example: Jordan texts: 'make the Instacart link for this week's list.'
how:
Gate first: Instacart must approve a production API key (see caveats). Then the shape is a small host-side tool plugin `home-cart` with one tool that takes no free-text arguments. It reads the grocery list itself (Reminders bridge F030 or home-store), calls Instacart's `POST /idp/v1/products/products_link` and returns `products_link_url`. Held by `

-main`. Not advised: adding Instacart's own remote MCP server to `

-main` (`openclaw mcp add ... --transport streamable-http --include 'create-shopping-list'`), because that tool takes model-written text and would be a third-party egress path on an agent that holds memory. The result is a URL.
depends_on: an Instacart Developer Platform API key
the family actually ordering through Instacart
an approved Instacart production API key (Instacart review required)
caveats: Zero value if the family's store is not on Instacart or they shop in person.
Instacart matches items by search term, so brand and size are approximate; the parent still edits the cart.
Needs a developer key; the application process was not checked.
A shared Reminders grocery list plus the store's own app is what most families use and needs no build.

Needs an Instacart production API key. Per Instacart's docs the key does not work until Instacart has reviewed the integration (terms, API usage, error handling, a help-desk account), and the average time from access request to production key is about 30 to 40 days. The process is written for apps and websites; a development key only reaches the development servers.
safety: No purchase, cart or checkout happens on Happy's side; the never-list holds because the tool can only produce a link. The risk is egress: a tool that posts model-written text to a third party is a way to send data out from an agent that holds memory. Close it by having the tool read the list itself and accept no free-text arguments; do not put Instacart's MCP server on a memory-holding agent. Item names still reach Instacart, and the returned link is shareable, so anyone holding it can see the list.
unverified: Ohai's Instacart connection: seen only on a non-canonical Ohai subdomain, so not cited.
How Instacart approves developer keys and whether a household can get one.
Whether the family uses Instacart.
Whether Instacart would approve a production key for one household's private tool.
Whether a link created with a development key opens a real, orderable Instacart page.

name: Teach Happy a routine (operator-reviewed skills)
description: A parent describes once how the family does something; it becomes a named skill Happy follows every time (party plan, ski-trip packing, school-form explainer). A skill goes live only after Tony has read it.
example: Happy, learn our ski-trip packing routine: ask how many nights and who is coming, then list by person, and always include the kids' helmets.
how:
Happy answers with the drafted procedure as plain text (no tool needed). Tony turns it into `skills//SKILL.md` (a `name` and a one-line `description`, optionally `user-invocable`) in happy-config under that person's template, reviews it, and happy-deploy copies it into that agent's workspace `skills/` folder, the highest-precedence skill root. To use a skill the model must load its SKILL.md with the `read` tool; the system prompt lists only each skill's name, description and location. So

-main needs `read` in `tools.alsoAllow` and in the sandbox tool allowlist (group:fs is denied today). With `workspaceAccess: "none"` OpenClaw mirrors eligible skills into the sandbox workspace as read-only copies and `read` is rooted there. Keep `skill_workshop` denied on every family agent. Alternative for agent-scoped Workshop skills: `openclaw skills workshop propose-create --agent

-main --proposal ./PROPOSAL.md`, then inspect and apply, run as the happy user from the deploy path. Per-agent visibility through `agents.entries..skills`; inbox keeps `skills: []`. Held by the asking parent's

-main; shared stateless agents get only skills meant for everyone. A routine of a few lines can instead live as a section of AGENTS.md, which needs no tool.
depends_on: a skills step in happy-deploy and gen-family
decision: who may request a new skill

`read` allowed on

-main in tools.alsoAllow and the sandbox tool allowlist (group:fs is denied today; arrives with F041)
caveats: Asking Happy to save a skill from iMessage does not work on this stack by default: sandboxed runs do not construct the `skill_workshop` tool even when it is allowlisted, so `/learn` cannot stage a draft. The M1 doctor baseline in the config repo already shows this warning for every agent. The documented exception is a human turn with host-granted library-authoring authority, and personal-library authoring publishes with no pending draft, which would skip Tony's review. That is one more reason to keep `skill_workshop` off every family agent's allowlist.
A skill is know-how. It cannot add tools or accounts, so "learn to order the groceries" still ends at a list.
A skill is instruction text loaded into future sessions. One written from a pasted web page or an email is a stored injection, so author only from the parent's own words.
No marketplace skills: an audit reported by The Hacker News found 341 malicious entries among 2,857 ClawHub skills in early 2026.
A running session keeps the skill list it started with; a new skill appears after /new or the next morning's reset.
Turnaround is "when Tony next deploys", not instant.
A new or changed workspace skill is picked up on the next turn after the skills watcher sees the file change, or after the gateway restart that a deploy performs. No /new is needed.
safety:
Operator review is the gate: no model-written file ever reaches a skills root. A skill cannot widen tool policy, so the trifecta split between

-main, research and the mail readers is unchanged. Per-person skills live in that person's workspace, so nothing crosses data domains.
unverified: Whether a user-invocable skill command typed by an allowlisted non-owner iMessage sender is accepted on 2026.9.7.
That skill sync into the sandbox works with `workspaceAccess: "none"` (the docs say sandboxed runs read materialized copies).

That a `read`-only grant on a sandboxed

-main reaches the mirrored skills and nothing private; check at build time.
Whether an iMessage owner turn is ever given library-authoring authority on this configuration. If it is, an allowlisted `skill_workshop` could publish a skill with no review.

name: Deep recall of earlier conversations (Active Memory)
description: When a parent asks about something from an earlier day, a short blocking recall step searches that same agent's own past private conversations and gives the answer a small summary to work from. It earns its keep on this stack because the conversation resets every morning.
example: What did we decide about the summer camp deposit last week?
how:
Per agent: `agents.entries.

-main.memory.search.rememberAcrossConversations: true` with the active-memory plugin enabled in its default `escalate` mode, which runs the recall sub-agent only when the message asks about the past and the cheap deterministic lookup found nothing strong. Direct chats only, same agent only. Held by each

-main; never on research, the readers, or inbox.
depends_on:
F041 memory path and memory tools on

-main
a check that the keyword-only memory provider supports transcript recall
decision: index session transcripts or not
a staging test that a pre-reset transcript of the same DM is recalled
caveats: It defaults to off on Happy because per-sender DM isolation is configured; it must be set explicitly per agent.
It adds a blocking model call to the replies it runs on: slower answers and extra cost.
It does not run for scheduled jobs, heartbeat or sub-agents, so the briefs get nothing from it.
Recalled excerpts come from transcripts that include search-tool output, and hidden personalization can surprise ("how did it know that").
A cheaper first step is already in the catalog: the session-memory hook plus memory search from F041. Try that before this.

Each parent has one private conversation with their agent (the iMessage DM). Recall reads the same agent's other private conversations and excludes the one being answered. Whether the pre-reset transcript of that same DM counts as another conversation is not documented; if it does not, this feature returns nothing on Happy. Test that before anything else.
safety: Recall stays inside one agent, which is one person: another agent's transcripts are never eligible and groups are excluded. The recall sub-agent can call only memory recall tools and nothing leaves the gateway beyond the model call the agent already makes. Treat recalled text as possibly tainted by earlier search results and keep the F041 rule that tainted turns cannot write memory.
unverified: Whether protected transcript recall works with `memory.search.provider: "none"` (keyword only, no embeddings).
Whether yesterday's pre-reset transcript of the same DM counts as another private conversation for recall.
The added latency and cost per recall on the models Happy uses.

review_notes: All six sources confirmed, but the stated payoff rests on behaviour nobody has tested: each parent has exactly one private conversation with their agent and recall excludes the conversation being answered. Unless yesterday's pre-reset transcript counts as another conversation there is nothing to recall, so readiness becomes experimental and value 2 until that test passes.

name: Dedicated school mailbox with isolated reader (school-mail) and forward-to-Happy
description: A separate mailbox registered with school, PTA, coaches and the lunch system, read by an isolated reader, so no parent's private inbox is touched; parents can forward mail to it.
how: Bundled `imap` plugin on a new mailbox (iCloud needs `watch.mode: "interval"`), allowlist includes both parents for forwards, tool-less reader; same delivery caveat as F050.
corrections: 'IMAP passes body text only' is slightly off: the plugin's prompt also lists attachment file names (dist/extensions/imap/index.js:55735). Contents of attached PDFs or images are still not passed, so flyer attachments remain unread.
unverified: Whether the district, PTA, coaches and lunch system each accept an extra or shared guardian address; this is a manual chore per system.

Auto-forwarding school mail from a parent's Gmail by filter may fail the plugin's aligned-DMARC check (Google's forwarding guidance says forwarded mail often fails SPF); DKIM survival was not tested, so registering the address directly is the safe route.
An iCloud+ custom-domain address with this plugin was not tested; Apple documents the IMAP host and app-specific passwords, not this combination.
The catalog marks this 'now' because it needs no private-inbox decision; I rate it 'build' because it needs a new mailbox, an app password and a reader agent entry.

sources.title: IMAP email trigger
sources.supports: Some iCloud servers do not advertise standard IDLE, so forcing interval polling (15 second minimum) is the supported path for an iCloud mailbox.

sources.title: IMAP plugin source: renderImapPrompt
sources.supports: The prompt handed to the reader contains From, Subject, a snippet, attachment file names and the capped text body; attachment contents are never included.

sources.title: Apple Support: iCloud Mail server settings for other email client apps
sources.supports: iCloud Mail is reachable over IMAP with SSL on port 993 and requires an app-specific password for third-party clients.

name: Sender allowlist and mail-rule management by chat
description: 'Trust mail from the new coach' produces a proposed allowlist change that the mailbox owner approves in chat, so the lists stay current without hand-editing config.
how: In-house tool proposes a diff; `requireApproval` gate answered with `/approve`; host code regenerates `plugins.entries.imap.config.accounts.*.allowedSenders`, which hot-applies without a restart.
corrections: The 9 Oct needs list names `openclaw config reload`; no such command appears in the installed docs, and `plugins.entries.*` changes hot-apply without a Gateway restart (docs/gateway/configuration/hot-reload.md:124).
unverified: Limiting who may approve to the mailbox owner, rather than any allowlisted family member, is in-house logic; I found no built-in per-approver rule in the pages read.

'Digest categories' and the weekly 'senders I ignored' line are prompt or home-store ideas, not plugin features; the plugin logs rejections without subjects or bodies (docs/automation/imap.md:170), so that line would have to be built from gateway logs.
Useless until a mailbox (F051 or the personal-inbox path) is connected.

Bundled `imap` plugin, `allowedSenders`, `senderAuth.min: verified`, tool-less `

-mail-reader`; Google app password as SecretRef; texting the owner needs a hook-pinned `message` tool or a cron sweep.

Whether each allowlisted sender's mail passes aligned DMARC has to be tested sender by sender.
An app password is a whole-mailbox credential, broader than a read-only OAuth grant; this is my reading of Google's description, not a quoted statement.

name:
Per-person mail reader agent (

-mail): isolated, memory-off, no web, deliver-to-owner only
description: One locked-down mail agent per adult: it can read that adult's mail and write drafts, cannot browse or run code, and can only message its owner.
how:
Agent entry with `profile: "minimal"`, explicit `

-gmail__*` allow plus the `tools.sandbox.tools` gate, deny web/fs/runtime/browser, owner-pinned send hook; checked with `openclaw sandbox explain --agent`.
corrections: The 9 Oct needs list omits the sandbox-layer gate: with sandbox mode 'all', MCP tools stay hidden unless `tools.sandbox.tools` names `bundle-mcp` or the server glob (docs/gateway/config-tools/tool-policy.md:101 and :130). The minimal profile does not allow MCP tools implicitly either (same file, lines 36 and 41).

'Memory off' is not one switch in the installed docs: memory search has a per-agent override (`agents.entries.*.memory.search`, `enabled`, docs/reference/memory-config.md:31 and :102), dreaming is plugin-wide (docs/concepts/memory.md:275), and `excludeSessions.hookExternalContentSources` only matches hook sessions (docs/reference/memory-config.md:667).

'Send pinned to owner' only applies when the mail agent runs its own scheduled or hook turn: when spawned from `

-main` it always loses `message` and `session_status` (docs/tools/subagents/tool-policy.md:23), so its allow list must not consist of `session_status` alone.
The 9 Oct needs list puts `openclaw models status --agent --probe` in the deploy checks; the installed doc says a direct probe needs the Gateway stopped (docs/cli/models.md:121).
unverified: The per-person provider setting that sends store false was verified in M1 and not re-read here.
Whether this OpenAI account has zero retention; without it the 30-day abuse-monitoring log applies to mail text sent to the model.
The promptfoo boundary canary is in-house.
A before_tool_call hook reaching MCP tool calls is implied by the doc ('every tool call in the run', docs/plugins/hooks/tool-policy.md:222) but I found no sentence naming MCP tools.

sources.title: IMAP email trigger
sources.supports: The doc's restricted reader template uses the minimal tool profile with an explicit allow list, denies file, runtime, web and browser tools, and runs fully sandboxed with no workspace access.

sources.supports: OpenAI states API data is not used for training by default, but abuse-monitoring logs can be kept up to 30 days unless the account is approved for zero retention, so store-off is not the same as nothing retained.

name:
Per-person read-only Gmail (

-gmail MCP)
description: Each adult's own mail agent can search and read that adult's Gmail; nothing is changed, labelled or sent.
how:
`gog mcp` as a host-side stdio entry under `mcp.servers`, read tools only, allowed per agent as `

-gmail__*`; authorize with `--gmail-scope readonly`.
corrections: The 9 Oct verifier note says gogcli has no read-only-only Gmail scope. The upstream command reference lists `--gmail-scope full|readonly|send|read-send` and says `--readonly` on `gog auth add` requests read-only OAuth scopes, so a read-only grant can be requested; the catalog's hedge 'if the installed version supports it' can be firmed up, pending a check on the installed binary.

The 9 Oct text treats the `

-gmail` wrapper as new code. Upstream gogcli ships a stdio MCP server (`gog mcp`) that exposes only read tools unless `--allow-write` is passed, so the config entry can run gog directly with an `--allow-tool` list and no wrapper.

The 9 Oct needs list stops at the per-agent allow list. With sandbox mode 'all' (Happy's setting) the installed docs add a second gate: MCP tools are filtered out unless `tools.sandbox.tools` also names `bundle-mcp` or the server glob (docs/gateway/config-tools/tool-policy.md:101 and :130).
unverified: gog is not installed on this Mac; the flags come from the upstream main-branch docs and must be confirmed with `gog mcp --list-tools` and `gog auth add --help` on the version Homebrew installs.

Whether both adults' tokens would sit in one keyring under the happy user: upstream says tokens use the platform keyring by default with a file backend for headless hosts; splitting them with a per-adult GOG_HOME is my inference from the paths doc.
Refresh-token lifetime for a self-made Google OAuth client left in testing status was not checked in this run; Google's scope page does mark gmail.readonly as a Restricted scope.
The promptfoo injection canary is an in-house test, not an OpenClaw feature.

sources.title: Connect MCP servers
sources.supports: MCP server definitions live in gateway config and the tools they expose pass through the same tool profile and policy controls as built-in tools.

sources.title: Multi-agent sandbox and tools
sources.supports: MCP tools get server-prefixed names that per-agent allow and deny lists can target, deny always wins, and a server with no allowed tool is omitted for that agent.

sources.title: gogcli docs: MCP server
sources.supports: gog ships its own typed stdio MCP server (`gog mcp`); by default it registers read tools only (Gmail search, get message, get thread) and hides every write tool.

sources.title: gogcli command reference: gog auth add
sources.supports: The authorization command takes a Gmail scope mode of full, readonly, send or read-send, and its --readonly flag requests read-only OAuth scopes.
